paragraphs: This list is for self-questioning only and does not constitute recruitment criteria, a capability score, or a conclusion evaluating construction quality and safety. This page is written according to the US O*NET-SOC 47-2043.00 'Floor Sanders and Finishers' (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name whose English rendering is 'Floor sanders and finishers'; the main objects are scraping, sanding and topcoat finishing of wooden floors).

Exercise prompt | a room of about 30 square metres with an old wooden floor needs renovation. Write a completely fictional work draft: (1) how to inspect the floor before starting (moisture content, cupping, gaps, type of old coating) and determine whether it is suitable for sanding; (2) how to choose the sequence of coarse sanding, fine sanding and edge sanding and the abrasive grits; (3) how to control dust removal and coating intervals (including ventilation and fire safety requirements); (4) how to carry out a completion self-check (surface flatness, colour variation, coating evenness and curing) and leave reviewable records. Use public information and simulated dimensions in your answer, and do not use any real client, address or contract information.

Fit signals | O*NET points of focus: using hands to handle, control or feel tools continuously (88% continually or almost continually), face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (83%), continuous bending or twisting of the body (76%), precision or accuracy extremely important (50%), a lot of freedom to determine tasks and priorities (51%), making decisions every day (55%), teamwork important (53%). If you are willing to operate sanding equipment and hand tools for long periods, to control the process finely according to abrasive and coating techniques, and are sensitive to surface flatness and colour variation, then the daily requirements of this occupation are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows: exposed to contaminants every day (90%), exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day (76%), exposed to hazardous equipment every day (59%), exposed to whole body vibration every day (44%), wearing specialised protective equipment every day (42%), exposed to hazardous conditions every day (35%), time pressure (53% once a week or more), pace determined by equipment speed (31% extremely important), continuous bending or twisting of the body (76%) and kneeling, crouching or crawling (66%). Sanding and coating work involves wood dust, solvent coating odours and high noise, and dust also carries an explosion risk. If you find it hard to wear protective equipment for long periods or to work in dust and solvent environments, or have low tolerance for sanding vibration, treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Taking on the judgement | real fit comes from being able to do three things at once in the real pace of a site: keep to the process steps (moisture content and suitability determination, coarse and fine sanding sequence, dust removal and coating intervals), make the surface stable (flat, free of sanding marks, even colour and coating), and take on reviewable record-keeping responsibility at process handovers. It is suggested to test this through one verifiable experience (such as working as a labourer or apprentice on a wooden floor renovation site, or a vocational school sanding and coating practical assessment), rather than relying only on the conclusion of an interest questionnaire.

Safety work sample (a completely fictional task pack): given a simulated floor plan of a room of about 30 square metres with an old wooden floor and a description of the old coating, complete a renovation work draft within 60 minutes: suitability check records (moisture content, cupping, gaps, type and thickness of the old coating), abrasive and process plan (grits and sequence for coarse sanding — fine sanding — edge sanding), dust removal and ventilation plan (including dust fire safety and solvent use requirements), coating interval and curing control, completion self-check sheet (flatness, sanding marks, colour variation, coating evenness and curing), and state clearly which situations must be paused and reported rather than handled on your own.

O*NET47-2043.00 is the use of scrapers and floor sanding machines to make wooden floors smooth and to apply coatings. Tasks include cleaning, scraping and sanding edges and corners, flatness checks, gap filling and coating, and it is distinguished from laying covering materials, carpet, ceramic and stone tiles and terrazzo. Actual structure, services, fire safety, environmental protection or old coating disposal qualifications are verified by project and jurisdiction, and the occupational classification is not a list of legal permits.

entries: Suitability determination | on-site inspection and judgement | verify the floor moisture content, cupping and deformation, gaps and looseness, and the type and thickness of the old coating to judge whether sanding conditions exist; floors with excessive moisture or structural deformation should have the conditions treated before work begins.

Surface scraping | removing old coatings and residual adhesive | use scrapers and edge grinding equipment to remove old paint, wax, adhesive and stains, handling edges and corners and areas the equipment cannot reach.

Mechanical sanding | abrasive sequence from coarse to fine | choose grits according to the equipment and floor condition and sand in stages to eliminate sanding marks and level the surface; control travel speed and overlap width to avoid hollows and waves.

Edges and hand work | hard-to-reach areas | use edge sanders, scrapers and sandpaper by hand on wall corners, door frames and areas near radiators to ensure a natural transition with the machine-sanded surface.

Dust removal and coating | sealing and coating | remove dust thoroughly and clean, and control coating intervals and curing per the instructions; after gap filling and filler repair, sand and remove dust again.

Self-check and handover | appearance and curing verification | check sanding marks, waves, colour variation, coating runs and curing, form a reviewable self-check record per the acceptance requirements, and state clearly the protection of the finished work and subsequent use restrictions.

paragraphs:
Work context | the O*NET 47-2043.00 work context shows: the work is characterised by hands-on operation, dust and solvent environments and high noise, with specific conditions varying by floor condition and site type.
Contaminant exposure | exposed to contaminants every day (90%), mainly wood dust and coating vapours, requiring ventilation and protection.
Hand use | using hands to handle, control or feel objects and tools continuously (88% continually or almost continually).

Face-to-face communication | face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (83%), requiring on-site confirmation of floor condition and process progress.
Physical load | continuous bending or twisting of the body (76%), kneeling, crouching or crawling (66%), and repetitive motion for long periods (66%).
Noise environment | exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day (76%), from sanding equipment and dust extraction equipment.

Protective equipment | wearing routine protective equipment every day (61%) and specialised protective equipment (42%), with hazardous equipment exposure 59% every day; these are the corresponding answer bands, not accident rates.
Decision authority | decision freedom partly free (55%), a lot of freedom to determine tasks and priorities (51%); precision or accuracy extremely important (50%).
Time and pace | time pressure exists (53% once a week or more but not every day), and pace is determined by equipment speed (31% extremely important).

Environment and pace | the work is mostly inside housing, offices and shops that are delivered or half delivered, usually after other trades have left the site; there is a lot of dust on site, limited ventilation, and noticeable coating odour and noise. The work pace is constrained by floor condition, coating curing time and the schedule for bringing in furniture, and overtime is needed to meet deadlines; the slow and busy seasons relate to regional renovation cycles. Physical load is concentrated in long periods of bending, kneeling and pushing and pulling equipment, and protective gear and dust extraction equipment must be used per procedure with attention to dust fire safety.

Tools and materials | equipment: drum sanders, flat sanders, edge sanders, scrapers and putty knives, dust extraction and dust removal equipment, gap filling and coating tools (rollers, brushes, spreaders). Materials: abrasive grits (sandpaper and abrasive cloth), filler and gap filling materials, primer and topcoat or penetrating coatings, cleaners and wax removers. Documents: floor and coating product instructions, moisture content and work condition descriptions, coating interval and curing time schedules, self-check and acceptance sheets. All process parameters (moisture content limits, coating intervals, curing times) are subject to the product instructions valid on the day.

Inspect floor and old coating condition → determine suitability and treat defects → coarse and fine sanding and finishing edges → dust removal and gap filling repair → coating and curing control → self-check handover and protecting the finished work

Quality standards | the surface should be flat and free of sanding marks and waves, with a natural transition between edges and machine-sanded surfaces; colour variation and coating thickness should be controlled, with even coating, no runs and no missed areas, and curing meeting the instructions. Dust should be removed thoroughly and the interior should reach delivery condition after work; moisture content and work conditions should meet product requirements. Anything inconsistent with the drawings, product instructions or acceptance specifications must be recorded and reported to the foreman and must not be downgraded on your own.

Adjacent responsibility boundaries | this page covers O*NET-SOC 47-2043.00; adjacent but different occupations include Floor Layers, Except Carpet, Wood, and Hard Tiles (resilient material laying), Carpet Installers (carpet), Tile and Stone Setters (ceramic and stone tiles), Terrazzo Workers and Finishers (terrazzo) and Carpenters (wood component work). Matters involving floor structure repair, replacement of wood components and floor waterproofing are borne by the corresponding trades and responsible parties; this occupation does not overstep to replace their judgement and sign-off.

Boundary review points | pause and escalate when the following situations arise: the floor moisture content exceeds the limit or there is structural deformation that cannot be treated per the instructions; the floor is judged unsuitable for sanding (such as too thin a wear layer, severe damage, or harmful materials requiring specialist handling); the old coating may contain regulated substances such as lead and needs specialist disposal (stop and hand it to a qualified person for assessment); on-site ventilation or fire safety conditions are insufficient; or structural changes or changes affecting fire compartments are needed. These situations are handled by the foreman, technical lead or project manager per the contract and specifications.

Inspect floor and old coating → determine suitability and treat defects → coarse and fine sanding and finishing edges → dust removal and gap filling → coating and curing → self-check and protection of the finished work

Difference from floor-layers-except-carpet-wood-and-hard-tiles: the latter lay covering materials such as resilient sheet, linoleum, cork and rubber on top of the substrate, and the delivery is a complete floor covering; this occupation scrapes, sands and coats the surface of existing wooden floors, and the delivery is a flat, coated wooden surface. The material systems, tools and acceptance indicators of the two differ.

Difference from carpet-installers: the latter handle the cutting, pattern matching and tensioning of soft carpet material; this occupation handles the sanding and coating of hard wooden surfaces and does not involve soft materials, and the process and finished appearance standards of the two differ.

Difference from tile-and-stone-setters: the latter lay hard blocks using wet work and emphasise void control and joint filling; this occupation does not lay blocks but sands and coats the surface of wooden floors, and the work conditions and acceptance indicators differ, so they cannot substitute for one another.

Difference from terrazzo-workers-and-finishers: terrazzo workers are involved in site-cast and sanded and polished terrazzo surface work, which is a stone-based composite surface; this occupation's object is wooden flooring and involves wood sanding and coating systems, so the materials and processes of the two differ clearly.

Before choosing this occupation, compare: the real tasks (floor type, difficulty of treating the old coating, coating system), qualification and training paths (on-the-job training and apprenticeship, relevant certificates), shifts and travel (moving with projects, possibly working away from home), physical and health costs (dust, solvent odour, noise, kneeling and vibration), and growth paths (skilled sander, team leader, quality inspection, coating technical work or taking on wooden floor renovation contracts). Employers and regions vary considerably and this should be verified against actual recruitment and site experience.

Responsibility boundaries cannot be inferred from the similarity of job titles: although all are 'floor' positions, laying covering layers, laying carpet, laying ceramic and stone tiles, terrazzo work and wooden floor sanding and coating differ in material properties, process parameters, hazard factors and acceptance standards. Cross-trade work requires relearning the process and specifications and cannot reuse the original trade's judgement and sign-off authority.

AI task exposure | digital tools may assist with area and abrasive usage estimation, process records and draft checklists, coating interval and curing time reminders, and photo and document archiving. But moisture content and suitability judgement, abrasive and process selection, dust removal and ventilation control, coating work and curing judgement, and finished work acceptance and quality sign-off remain with the on-site workers and the foreman; task exposure does not equal job replacement.

Adoption conditions | digital tools entering a construction site need to satisfy: tool outputs are traceable and reviewable and do not replace on-site measurement; records and reminders do not encroach on actual work and safe dust removal time; estimates involving schedule and material usage must be confirmed by the foreman before being used for purchasing and settlement. A technical demonstration does not mean the organisation has adopted it, nor does it change coating work safety and environmental responsibility.

Data and system thresholds | before adoption, verify: whether the floor and coating instruction versions are controlled; whether moisture content and work condition records can be traced back to the original measurement; record access permissions and retention periods; whether devices or software can be used offline on sites without network; whether the data definitions are consistent between the different parties; and whether judgements involving regulated old materials such as lead can be traced back to their basis.

Human control points and manual review | suitability judgement, abrasive and process selection, dust removal and ventilation and fire safety control, coating work and curing judgement, and finished quality sign-off and process handover must be completed by the on-site workers and the foreman; any usage, interval or inspection conclusion generated by a tool must be manually reviewed with a trace of the check left before use.

Residual responsibility | matters that must not be released automatically: whether the floor has sanding conditions, whether the old coating needs specialist disposal, whether the coating system and intervals apply, whether the finished work meets the acceptance standards, and confirmation of changes and additional costs. No tool output equals a pass conclusion or an authorisation decision.

Failure risk | unreviewed tool outputs may directly cause wrong abrasive and coating usage, reversed process sequence, misjudged curing times and rework, or treating unconfirmed condition judgements as an established plan on site, resulting in surface defects, coating failure and cost overruns. Before deployment, make clear who reviews and against what original materials.

Employment evidence boundaries | the employment and wage data of this occupation must be distinguished by definition: the US figures from O*NET and the BLS are estimates under a specific statistical definition and cannot be extrapolated directly to mainland China or other regions; China uses industry category average wages as a background proxy, which does not constitute an occupational wage conclusion. Anything generated should be traceable back to the original inputs and sources, and fluent wording must not be treated as correct evidence.

Practical response | first put digital tools into low-risk steps that can be rolled back and audited (such as record organisation and photo archiving, usage trial calculations and curing reminders), subject to on-site measurement and foreman confirmation; decide whether to expand the scope of use based on error records and rework, and always keep manual sign-off for safety and quality judgements.

Cross-market definition boundaries | mainland China and the United States have different industry and occupational classification systems: mainland China publishes the average wage of employed persons in urban units by national economic industry category, without listing this occupation separately; the United States gives estimates by SOC occupation and industry. The two cannot be spliced or converted, and industry averages cannot replace occupational wages.

Insufficient evidence: mainland China has not established public occupational wage statistics precisely corresponding to 'floor sanders and finishers'; industry averages, recruitment quotes or third-party estimates are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence review points | this page provides only statistical definitions, industry background proxies and a register of visible gaps, and does not provide an estimated wage for this occupation. Before using any figure, first confirm whether its statistical definition (industry category / occupation), statistical period, unit of measurement and covered population are comparable with this occupation.

US wage evidence review points | the US figures on this page come from BLS OEWS May 2025 and the BLS 2024—2034 employment projections (presented via O*NET). Before use, confirm their occupational scope (SOC 47-2043), whether they include overtime and benefits (OEWS does not), and whether they are national rather than a single region or employer.

Mainland China wage evidence — market definition | the National Bureau of Statistics publishes the average wage of employed persons in urban units by industry category, which is a national urban unit definition and is not split by occupation; the average wages of related categories such as construction can only serve as background reference and cannot replace occupational wages.

Insufficient evidence: no occupational wage median for floor sanders and finishers that can be verified by occupation was obtained for mainland China; industry category averages are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence — statistical period | industry average wages are an annual definition (the figures below are for 2025, published in 2026), which differs from the US May 2025 point-in-time wage on this page, and the two periods cannot be mixed.

Cross-market definition boundaries | mainland China industry average wages and US occupational wages differ in statistical object, period and definition; this page presents them separately with their limitations noted, does not perform currency conversion, and does not treat industry averages as occupational wages.

Mainland China wage evidence — unit of measurement | the National Bureau of Statistics publishes annual average wages in 'yuan / year', on a pre-tax total wage definition (including personal income tax withheld by the employer and the employee's own social insurance and housing provident fund contributions); US OEWS publishes in 'US dollars / hour' or 'US dollars / year', excluding overtime, bonuses and benefits. The units and inclusions differ and cannot be compared directly.

Insufficient evidence: no floor sander and finisher wage data verifiable by region or employment form was obtained for mainland China; individual quotes or second-hand accounts are not used as substitutes.

Mainland China wage evidence — covered population | the urban non-private unit definition covers employed persons in non-private legal entities in urban areas, and the urban private unit definition covers employed persons in private units; neither covers self-employment, scattered contracting or the labour employment common in the renovation sector; income for this occupation varies considerably across employment forms and is hard for public statistics to cover.

US wage evidence — market definition | BLS OEWS is a sample survey estimate representing wages reported by employers; it excludes the self-employed. The median represents the midpoint of the distribution and is not a starting wage, nor does it represent any single region or employer.

US wage evidence — statistical period | the wage is May 2025 OEWS; employment, growth and openings are from the 2024—2034 employment projections. The two types of data have different reference points and must not be mixed into a conclusion for the same point in time.

US wage evidence — unit of measurement | published in 'US dollars / hour' and 'US dollars / year'; the annual average wage is converted on a full-year full-time basis, and converting between hourly and annual values does not equal personal actual income, which is also affected by hours, overtime and season.

US wage evidence — covered population | covers employed persons reported by non-farm establishment employers, excluding the self-employed, some agricultural positions and unreported cash-settled work; the independent contracting and daily-cash casual work common in renovation and refurbishment are hard to cover completely.

US wage evidence — occupational scope | the figures on this page correspond to SOC 47-2043 (Floor Sanders and Finishers); they exclude floor covering laying (47-2042), carpet installation (47-2041), tile and stone setting (47-2044) and terrazzo workers. Wages across occupations must not be mixed.

US wage evidence — sampling and missing data limitations | OEWS is a sample estimate with sampling error, and estimates may be missing or unreliable at industry and regional detail; this occupation has a small employment size (about 5,600 people in 2024), so detailed estimates are more prone to being missing; no industry-readable industry wage was obtained for this page, and that position is registered as a visible gap; industry averages or third-party estimates are not used as substitutes.

paragraphs: Conclusion | the core difference between this occupation and adjacent occupations lies in 'what is done to the surface of existing wooden floors': this occupation scrapes, sands and applies topcoats, delivering a flat, coated wooden surface; floor layers lay resilient covering materials on the substrate, carpet installers handle soft carpet material, tile and stone setters do wet-work laying, terrazzo workers produce site-cast and polished composite surfaces, and carpenters process wood components. The material systems, process parameters, hazard factors and acceptance standards all differ, and judgement and sign-off authority cannot be carried across trades.

Evidence note | the comparison objects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and publicly available materials on sale, and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent trades and choose a fit; they do not constitute qualification, recruitment or compensation conclusions. The wages and employment of each occupation must be verified separately under their own SOC definitions, and this table does not compare figures or treat one trade's wage as a proxy for another's.

Preface | the following comparison is laid out in four columns: 'occupational direction — core work and outputs — key differences — what it is a better choice for'. There is process linkage between adjacent trades (for example, the carpenter completes the wooden floor installation and this occupation sands and coats it, or this occupation finishes and the floor layer lays resilient material), but linkage does not equal substitutability; when choosing across directions, the process, specifications and acceptance standards must be relearned.

Wood surface treatment and the coating system are key: moisture content and suitability judgement, abrasive sequence, and dust removal and coating intervals determine the finished quality, and the process sequence cannot be reversed.

Better suited to people willing to operate sanding equipment for long periods, who can accept dust and solvent environments, and who are sensitive to surface flatness and colour variation; those interested in wood and coating systems fit better.

Output is a flat, coated wooden surface: suitability checks, scraping off the old coating, coarse and fine sanding, edge finishing, dust removal and gap filling, coating and curing, and finished work self-check.
This occupation: floor sanders and finishers

Laying resilient and soft covering materials on the substrate is key: it emphasises material expansion, jointing methods and adhesive open time, and it is 'laying a new surface layer' rather than 'treating an old wooden surface'.

Better suited to people who prefer material laying and jointing and edge finishing and are unwilling to face dust and coating odour for long periods; those with little interest in wood sanding and coating can choose this direction.

Output is a complete floor covering with joints and edge finishing: substrate inspection and treatment, setting out and trial laying, cutting and jointing and laying, edge transition, cleaning and self-check records.
Floor layers (except carpet, wood and hard tiles)

Cutting, pattern matching and tensioning of soft carpet material are key: it works with soft materials, and the finished work emphasises feel underfoot and decorative patterns, with no wood sanding or coating system involved.
Better suited to people who prefer soft materials and pattern matching; those interested in patterns and cutting and joining can choose this direction.
Output is a carpet-type covering: carpet cutting and pattern matching, seams and fixing, stair and doorway edge finishing, cleaning and acceptance records.
Carpet installers
Cutting, laying and joint filling of hard blocks are key: it is mostly wet work and is stricter about substrate strength and void control, with no wood or coating involved.
Better suited to people who can accept wet work and cutting dust and who enjoy finely controlling voids and joint appearance.
Output is a ceramic and stone surface: setting out and cutting, laying and levelling, joint filling and pointing, finished work protection and acceptance records.
Tile and stone setters

Forming a composite surface by site casting and sanding and polishing is key: it involves cement-based materials and aggregate proportions, dividing strips and grinding and polishing, adding casting and curing steps compared with this occupation.
Better suited to people who can accept both wet work and mechanical sanding and polishing and are willing to deal with proportions and curing.
Output is a terrazzo surface: substrate treatment, aggregate and cement proportions, casting and dividing, grinding, polishing and curing.
Terrazzo workers and finishers

Wood component processing and installation are key: the output is frames, doors and windows, cabinets and wood components; this occupation only treats the wooden surface after they are completed and does not take on component processing or structural duties.

Better suited to people willing to learn carpentry processing and dimensional fitting and able to take responsibility for component precision; those who only want surface treatment and coating fit this occupation.
Output is wood components and installation: measuring and setting out, component processing and assembly, installation and alignment, finished work and safety records.
Carpenters

Transition | this page sets adjacent trades side by side by material and process, to help you judge which craft you want to invest in long term. Whichever direction you choose, what really determines whether you can take up the work is your understanding of product instructions and acceptance specifications, on-site measurement and record-keeping capability, and passing a practical assessment accepted by the employer or foreman; an interest questionnaire is only for raising questions.

entries.answer: According to O*NET-SOC 47-2043.00, this occupation uses scrapers and sanding machines to scrape and sand wooden floors to make the surface flat and applies multiple topcoat layers. The work includes suitability checks (moisture content, cupping, type of old coating), scraping off the old coating, coarse and fine sanding, edge finishing, dust removal and gap filling, coating and curing control, and finished work self-check. It does not include laying floor covering materials, carpet, ceramic and stone tiling or terrazzo work.
entries.question: What does this occupation actually do?

entries.answer: Floor layers lay resilient and soft covering materials on the substrate, and the delivery is a new floor covering; carpenters process and install wood components (frames, doors and windows, the wooden floor itself, etc.); this occupation scrapes, sands and applies topcoats to the wooden surface after the wooden floor is installed, and the delivery is a flat, coated wooden surface. The material systems, process parameters and acceptance standards all differ.
